newsitem.title: USA: U.S.-Japan reach deal on port dispute.
newsitem.headline: U.S.-Japan reach deal on port dispute.

text.p: The United States and Japan reached a deal on Friday in a long-running dispute over access to Japanese ports, averting the imposition of U.S. sanctions scheduled to take effect on Monday.
The two countries signed a Memorandum of Consultation addressing the major issues discussed during 10 days of talks, Maritime Administrator Albert Herberger said late on Friday.

"Just-completed maritime discussions between the U.S. and Japanese governments were conducted in good faith and represent a reasonable basis for not imposing sanctions otherwise scheduled to go into effect April 14," he said in a written statement.

On that day, the U.S. Federal Maritime Commission had said it would impose penalties of $100,000 per visit on Japanese carriers calling at American ports if Tokyo did not move quickly to open access to Japanese ports.
The United States contends its shipping firms are treated unfairly by Tokyo, which maintains tight controls on the licensing of stevedores and port operations in Japan.
U.S. firms want to be able to hire their own stevedores and set up their own operations, claiming they could save money and improve productivity.
Herberger said the Japanese side agreed to approve applications from U.S. carriers for operations at Japan's berths and to deregulate the licensing system for port transportation business.
"The U.S. side said it is essential to complete deregulation ... as soon as possible, but no later than December 1998," he added.

On the issue of competition for stevedoring services in Japan, negotiators endorsed an interim agreement providing a framework for reforming the system by July 31, Herberger said. He gave no details of the plan.
Earlier, the U.S. State Department signalled that Washington wanted to conclude the talks before the deadline.

"We have said that if there no action by Monday, April 14, the Federal Maritime Commission will be forced to charge Japanese liners $100,000 if they visit our ports because there have been discriminatory practices against our own liners," spokesman Nicholas Burns told reporters.
The penalties were imposed by the commission in February after the two countries failed to resolve the five-year-old dispute.
